1: Missing values: mechanisms and imputation. Lectures seventeen and eighteen, with the matching lab, from Module three, data quality engineering and anomaly management.
2: Today's agenda has two parts. The lecture, why missing values happen and how to fix them: the three mechanisms, M C A R, M A R and M N A R; detection methods; and three imputation methods, mean or median, K N N, and regression based. The lab, imputing real missing data: detect and explain the missingness, impute with mean, median, K N N and regression, compare the strategies, and analyse the change in variance.
3: Why do missing values matter? No real dataset arrives complete. Forms get skipped, sensors drop out, and some values simply do not exist yet. Dropping every incomplete row throws away information, and filling blindly can distort the very statistics you are trying to compute. The right fix depends on why a value is missing, and that is what today's three mechanisms are for. In today's lab dataset, twenty point six percent of listings are missing reviews per month, and every single one has a clean, verifiable explanation. We will prove it in the M A R slide, and then fix it four different ways in the lab.
4: Every missing value fits one of three patterns, and the pattern determines whether an imputation method will help or quietly mislead you. M C A R, missing completely at random: missingness has no relationship to any variable, pure chance, like a random equipment glitch. M A R, missing at random: missingness depends on another observed column, not on the hidden value itself, like income missing more often for younger respondents. M N A R, missing not at random: missingness depends on the missing value itself, and cannot be verified from the data alone, like high earners declining to report income.
5: Mechanism one: M C A R, missing completely at random. The chance a value is missing has no relationship to any variable, observed or unobserved. It is noise, a coin flip unrelated to the data. In the New York Airbnb data, name is missing for sixteen listings and host name for twenty one, tiny, scattered counts with no obvious link to price, borough or any other column. This is consistent with M C A R, a host who simply left an optional field blank. But notice the careful wording: consistent with, not proven. M C A R can never be confirmed from data alone, only shown to be consistent with it, formally through Little's M C A R test. Absence of a pattern is not proof there is none.
6: Mechanism two: M A R, missing at random. The chance a value is missing depends on another observed column, not on the missing value itself. Condition on that column, and the missingness looks random. In this dataset, reviews per month is missing for ten thousand one hundred sixteen listings. We checked: every single one of those rows also has number of reviews equal to zero. That is not a coincidence, it is the definition of M A R. A listing with zero reviews has no reviews per month rate to record, so the missingness is fully explained by a column we already have. A hundred percent of the missing rows have zero reviews, a textbook, verified M A R relationship, not a guess.
7: Mechanism three: M N A R, missing not at random. The chance a value is missing depends on the missing value itself, and no amount of conditioning on other observed columns explains it away. As a hypothetical: imagine some hosts leave price blank specifically because it is unusually high or low, and they would rather not disclose it. Then the missingness would depend on the very value we cannot see. We cannot test this from the data alone. It needs domain knowledge, or asking the hosts directly. This is exactly why a completeness audit should never assume missing means random. Always check for M A R first. Price has no missing values in our dataset, so this is illustrative, not a finding. Another example: patients with the most severe symptoms are the likeliest to drop out of a trial before the final visit.
8: Detection methods. Detecting missing values is easy. Detecting why they are missing, which mechanism you face, is what decides your fix. First, count and percentage: df dot isnull dot sum, and df dot isnull dot mean times one hundred, the first, fastest scan of every column. Second, a visual pattern check: a missingness matrix or heatmap shows whether columns go missing together, in blocks, or scattered. Third, a conditional comparison: cross tabulate missingness against another column, which is exactly how we proved the M A R relationship.
9: Imputation, three strategies and three trade offs. Imputation replaces a missing value with an estimate. Every method trades simplicity against how much of the data's real structure it preserves. Mean or median is best as a quick baseline on roughly symmetric data, but it shrinks variance, since every fill is identical. K N N is best when features correlate with the missing one, like estimating a home's price from nearby similar homes, but it is slower on large data and needs scaled features. Regression based is best when there is a clear linear relationship, like predicting salary from years of experience, but it can extrapolate poorly outside the training range.
10: Imputation method one: mean or median. Replace every missing value with the column's mean for symmetric data, or median for skewed data. It is fast and simple, but every imputed row gets the exact same number. Why median fits our column: reviews per month is heavily right skewed, with a skew of about three point one, so a handful of very active listings pull the mean well above where most listings sit. For skewed data, the median is the more representative single number. Mean imputation drags every filled row toward that inflated average. Either way, filling with one constant flattens the column's natural spread. Mean fill kept seventy nine point four percent of the original variance, and median fill kept eighty two percent.
11: Imputation method two: K N N. For each missing value, find the k most similar rows using the other features, then average their observed values. It captures relationships a single constant never can. In our lab data, every missing reviews per month row also has zero reviews, our verified M A R relationship. K N N does not know that rule, but it still finds similar listings by price, location and availability, and its filled values average just point four one for those rows. Compare that to a blind mean fill of one point three seven for the same rows. K N N implicitly respects the M A R structure without being told. It retained eighty six point seven percent of the variance, the best of the four methods.
12: Imputation method three: regression based. Train a regression model on rows where the target is observed, using the other columns as predictors, then predict the missing values. It captures linear relationships explicitly. In our lab data, a linear model trained on price, location, availability and number of reviews explains only about thirty three percent of reviews per month, a modest fit. Because most training rows already had reviews, the model overshoots for the zero review rows, predicting a mean of point seven eight for them, well above K N N's more grounded point four one. It retained eighty one point nine percent, similar to median fill. Regression is powerful when the relationship is genuinely linear, but a weak R squared is a warning sign, not a free pass.
13: The lab begins, on the same dataset, picking up where lab fifteen and sixteen left off. Forty nine thousand one hundred ninety five listings, sixteen columns, twenty point six percent missing reviews per month, and a verified M A R mechanism. This is the exact file the duplicate removal and standardisation lab cleaned. Its real missing values were left untouched on purpose, because they are today's subject. Every number on the slides that follow comes from actually running this code on this file.
14: Lab step one: missing value detection. Count, locate and explain the missingness before imputing anything. Df dot isnull dot sum gives the count per column. Isnull mean times one hundred gives the percentage. And the cross tab of reviews per month being null against number of reviews equal to zero is the M A R test. It turns a guess, probably M A R, into a verified fact. Results: reviews per month and last review are each missing in ten thousand one hundred sixteen rows, twenty point six percent. Name and host name are missing in sixteen and twenty one. And all ten thousand one hundred sixteen missing rows have zero reviews, a hundred percent.
15: Step two: mean and median imputation. Compute the fill value from the observed rows only, then fillna applies it to every missing row in the column at once, with no loop. The observed variance is two point eight two four, with a mean of one point three seven three and a median of point seven one. Mean fill gives a variance of two point two four three, seventy nine point four percent retained. Median fill gives two point three one five, eighty two percent retained.
16: Step three: K N N imputation. K N N Imputer looks across all the listed columns at once to find each row's nearest neighbours, then averages their reviews per month, still one call and no loop. The predictors are price, minimum nights, number of reviews, availability, host listings count, latitude and longitude, with five neighbours. The new column's variance is two point four four eight, eighty six point seven percent retained. For the rows that were missing, K N N's average fill is point four one reviews per month, versus the blind mean fill of one point three seven. K N N implicitly knows these are low activity listings.
17: Step four: regression based imputation. Fit a linear regression on the rows where the target is observed, predict for the rows where it is missing, and clip at zero, since a review rate cannot be negative. The model fit on observed rows has an R squared of point three two nine, modest. The predicted mean for the missing rows is point seven eight reviews per month, and the new column's variance is two point three one three, eighty one point nine percent retained.
18: Step six: analyse the variance change. Every imputation method shrank the column's variance, because filling in a guess can never add real spread, only remove it. The question is how much. We loop over the four method columns, only four names, and compute each variance divided by the observed variance. Mean retains seventy nine point four percent, median eighty two, regression eighty one point nine, and K N N eighty six point seven. K N N loses the least variance, thirteen point three percent, because each row gets a locally grounded estimate. Mean fill loses the most, twenty point six percent, since all ten thousand one hundred sixteen rows get one identical number.
19: Step five: compare the imputation strategies. Same missing rows, four different fills. The observed only baseline has a mean of one point three seven three and variance two point eight two four. Mean fill: constant one point three seven three, variance two point two four three. Median fill: constant point seven one, new mean one point two three seven, variance two point three one five. K N N with five neighbours: varies per row, new mean one point one seven six, variance two point four four eight. Regression: varies per row, new mean one point two five two, variance two point three one three. K N N comes closest to the observed variance because it fills each row with a value grounded in similar listings, not one number repeated ten thousand times.
20: Key takeaways. Three mechanisms, M C A R, M A R and M N A R, describe why a value is missing, and that answer should drive your fix. A cross tab against an observed column is how you prove M A R, not guess it. A hundred percent of our missing rows had zero reviews. Mean and median imputation is the simplest fix and the biggest variance loss, seventeen to twenty one percent, since it fills every row with one identical number. K N N and regression both use the other columns to estimate a value. K N N preserved the most variance, eighty six point seven percent, and stayed closest to what the M A R structure implied. And always compare strategies and check the variance change, because a method that looks fine on the mean can still quietly flatten the data's spread.
